## Results

Synthesis and characterization of Fe-FER zeolite
Fe-FER zeolites have been successfully prepared using the hydrothermal synthesis method by means of ligand-stabilized metallic species precursors mixed with synthesis gel during the crystallization. Pyrrolidine is a preferred organic structure direct agent (OSDA) of FER zeolite to complex with iron ions, enabling to achieve atomically dispersion of Fe sites in crystalline zeolite. As shown in Fig. 1a, 0.6Fe-FER zeolite, as a representative sample, exhibits a typical plate-like shape of FER zeolite and no bright nanoparticles can be observed by HAADF-STEM image, despite highly dispersed Fe sites existing in the FER zeolite, as corroborated by the energy dispersive X-rays spectra (EDS) mapping images. Spherical aberration-corrected HAADF-STEM technology was exploited to further investigate the state of Fe sites. The microporous of zeolite, along with eight-membered ring channels, can be clearly visualized, and the bright spots observed at the higher accelerating current reveal the presence of atomically dispersed Fe sites in the 0.6Fe-FER zeolite. Nevertheless, highly dispersed tiny nanoparticles gradually appear as the iron content increases to 1.2 wt%. The UV–vis spectra of 1.2Fe-FER also reveal the presence of small oligomeric Fe O clusters at 346 nm, in addition to isolated Fe ion sites at 226 and 272 nm. X-ray absorption near edge structure (XANES) of Fe K-edge for the samples with Fe contents of 0.4, 0.6 and 1.2 wt% are closer to that of the reference Fe O , suggesting that Fe3+ is the major component in Fe-FER zeolites. Although linear combination analysis (LCA) of XANES spectra is a straightforward and widely used method in catalysis for estimating the Fe3+/Fe2+ ratio, the use of well defined reference compounds such as bulk oxides as standards often fails to accurately replicate the XANES features of actual catalyst samples due to differences in local coordination environments. The pre-edge peak in the spectra corresponds to the dipole-forbidden 1s→3d transition. The position of the pre-edge peak can also be used as a direct measure of the Fe oxidation state, making an unambiguous distinction between Fe2+ (~7112.5 eV) and Fe3+ (~7113.5 eV). Graphical analysis of the correlation between integrated intensities and positions of pre-edge features in the variogram was employed to further discriminate various oxidation states and coordination environments of Fe. Since the 1s→3d transition is a quadrupolar transition, it exhibits weak intensity in coordination geometries with an inversion center (centrosymmetric geometry), such as octahedral coordination. But in fivefold or fourfold geometry, 3d–4p orbital hybridization facilitates dipole-allowed 1s→4p transitions, resulting in significantly higher intensity. As shown in Fig. 1c and Fig. 1d, the higher integrated intensities of Fe-FER zeolites pre-edge analysis than Fe3+ Oh, indicating that Fe sites in a lower geometry in Fe-FER zeolites than the bulk α-Fe O . The Fe3+/Fe2+ ratio obtained by curve fitting analysis of pre-edge peak in Fe-FER zeolites exhibits an increasing trend with increasing iron loading. It can also be demonstrated in the phase-uncorrected Fourier transform X-ray absorption fine structure (FT-EXAFS) spectra that the first contribution of Fe-FER zeolites is closer to the Fe-O scattering path and the absence of the second contribution demonstrates that Fe sites are highly dispersed in FER-zeolites in the form of coordination with oxygen. According to curve-fitting results as shown in Table S3, the average distance and coordination number of Fe-O for 0.6Fe-FER zeolite are estimated to be 2.05 Å and 4.7, respectively, which are consistent with the results of pre-edge analysis. Although the Fe–O–Fe peaks are clearly observed in α-Fe O , they are difficult to detect in the second-shell contributions of zeolite catalysts when the metal species or oxide particles are very small and highly dispersed. As for the FT-EXAFS spectra of 1.2Fe-FER, similarly, the absence of the second contribution can also be perceived, demonstrating that although the presence of nanoparticles in 1.2Fe-FER, they are still highly dispersed as iron oxide nanoparticles without any apparent agglomeration. Moreover, the absence of higher R-space signals by the wavelet transform analysis also validate the high dispersion of Fe sites.

Mössbauer spectroscopy is an effective technique to provide reliable information on the forms of iron sites and the environment where iron ions exist in zeolite by measuring the hyperfine interaction between nuclear moments and electromagnetic fields. Consequently, Mössbauer spectroscopy was further employed to precisely characterize the Fe sites in 57Fe-FER zeolites. Mössbauer spectra are shown in Fig. 1f, and the corresponding Mössbauer parameters are listed in Table 1. The species and locations of iron can be pinpointed by the hyperfine parameters of isomer shift (IS) and quadrupole splitting (QS). Typically, 0.1 ≤ IS < 0.6 mm/s and 0.6 ≤ IS ≤ 1.4 mm/s are assignable to Fe3+ and Fe2+ component, respectively. The value of QS is correlated with symmetry. Larger QS values represent the worse symmetry around iron ions. As shown in Table 1, the spectral contributions of Fe-FER samples advocate that Fe3+ is the major component in Fe-FER zeolites. Concomitantly, based on the results of 27Si MAS NMR and 27Al MAS NMR, the introduction of Fe3+ has no effect on the framework of zeolite, indicating that Fe3+ is primarily in the extra-framework of zeolite. FER zeolite comprises ten-membered ring channels (4.2×5.4 Å) intersected by eight-membered ring channels (3.5×4.8 Å). As depicted in Fig. 1g, four characteristic positions denoted as B, C, F, and G can be occupied by isolated cations in FER zeolite as reported in previous literatures and the C-sites remain unoccupied at low iron concentration.

Three kinds of iron sites were found to be present in the 0.4Fe-FER and 0.6Fe-FER zeolites. The component I of 0.4Fe-FER zeolite with IS=0.28 mm/s and QS=1.53 mm/s and 0.6Fe-FER zeolite with IS=0.25 mm/s and QS=1.7 mm/s can be assigned to the [FeO]+ at the six-membered ring (G-site). The component II of 0.4Fe-FER zeolite with IS=0.52 mm/s and QS=2.83 mm/s and 0.6Fe-FER zeolite with IS=0.5 mm/s and QS=2.8 mm/s has a high value of QS, suggesting that the component is in a position that confers it less symmetry. Accordingly, the Fe3+ at the B-site can be assigned to the component II, as reported previously. The component III of the Fe-FER zeolites with IS>0.6 mm/s is assigned to Fe2+, while the lower value of QS (<0.5 mm/s) indicates that Fe2+ is most likely located at the G-site and stabilized with the negative charge provided by the two aluminum. Compared to 0.4Fe- and 0.6Fe-FER zeolite, the component IV with IS=0.30 mm/s and QS=1.10 mm/s was observed in the 1.2Fe-FER zeolite, which is assignable to the tiny Fe O nanoparticles in accordance with the results of TEM and the reference. Collectively, single Fe3+ sites consist mainly of [FeO]+ at G-sites and Fe3+ at B-sites in Fe-FER zeolites, whereas tiny Fe O nanoparticles appear as the Fe content increases to 1.2 wt%. The perturbed T-O-T vibrational modes (1000~800 cm−1 in the IR spectra) of the zeolite framework also provide an effective method to distinguish different Fe sites. The IR bands at 903, 895, 885, and 873 cm−1 are attributed to T-O-T oxygen bridges perturbed by Fe2+, Fe3+, [FeO]+, and small oligomeric Fe O clusters, respectively. The quantitative results are in good agreement with those obtained from the Mössbauer spectra.

The exploitation of 2D 1H-1H DQ MAS NMR spectroscopy has enriched the material characterization methods at the atomic scale, allowing for in-depth exploration of the proximity between active sites, which has often been interpreted as ‘the closer the better’ for locating metal and acid sites. Two off-diagonal cross-peak pairs at (4.0, 6.7) and (2.7, 6.7) ppm, as well as (2.9, 5.4) and (2.5, 5.4) ppm corresponding to the adjacent Si-O(H)-Al sites (BASs) and EFAL species (Al-OH) can be distinguished in H-FER zeolite, in addition to the diagonal autocorrelation peaks corresponding to close proximity of Si-O(H)-Al sites at (3.9, 7.8) ppm and silanols at (1.7, 3.4) ppm. The absence of autocorrelation peak at (3.9, 7.8) ppm in Fe-FER zeolites regardless of the amount of iron as shown in Fig. 2b–d suggests that Fe sites prefer to occupy one of the adjacent Si-O(H)-Al sites, resulting in the disappearance of autocorrelation peaks of BASs, as depicted in Fig. 2e. The reduced amount of BASs and enhanced amount of LASs in Fe-FER zeolites quantified by the FT-IR spectra of NH adsorption also confirm that Fe sites, substituting proton counter-cations, exhibit Lewis acid properties by acting as electron pair acceptors. The amounts of BASs determined by the Al sites framework are consistent with the results obtained from the FT-IR spectra of NH adsorption. Moreover, the content of Si-O(H)-Al sites at 3.9 ppm decreases 54% to 20% as the iron content increases in 1H MAS NMR results and the reduction of desorption band at 300~600 °C measured by temperature-programmed desorption of NH (NH -TPD) experiment also suggesting that Si-O(H)-Al sites are partially occupied by Fe sites. No significant difference is observed before 650 °C between the TCD and MS signals, indicating that ammonia decomposition does not occur in Fe-FER zeolites. The BASs formed by framework aluminum in zeolites are primarily located within the internal channels. The introduction of iron species mainly exists as ion sites that replace BASs and are incorporated into the zeolite channels. In contrast, EFAL species are also distributed on the external surface of the zeolite. Therefore, the introduction of iron has a more significant impact on the BASs compared to the EFAL species.

Catalytic performance of Fe-FER zeolites
Since the excellent redox properties are crucial for the SCR reaction, the NO oxidation performance of the Fe-FER zeolites was first investigated. The conversion of NO increases gradually can be observed with the increment of iron content and the activation energy for NO oxidation of the 0.6Fe-FER zeolite (E = 31.2 kJ/mol) is lower than that of the H-FER zeolite (E = 56.6 kJ/mol), suggesting that the introduction of Fe sites is conducive to the oxidation of NO. Concomitantly, investigations were steered towards the correlation between the content of different Fe sites and the reaction rate of NO oxidation. The reaction rates for NO oxidation, which excludes the limitations of internal and external diffusion, manifest an immensely good linear relationship with the amount of [FeO]+ present in Fe-FER zeolites. On the contrary, neither the amount of the Fe3+ nor the Fe2+ correlates with the reaction rate of NO. Reaction order with respect to NO was measured over the 0.6Fe-FER zeolite by analyzing the reaction rate dependency on reactant concentration. As shown in Fig. S14, the reaction rate was found to have linear dependence with respect to NO, with the slope of the linear fit being approximately 1, indicating that the reaction follows first-order kinetics.

In situ Mössbauer and FT-IR spectroscopy were employed to monitor the changes of Fe sites during the NO oxidation reaction. Mössbauer spectra are shown in Fig. 3c and the corresponding Mössbauer parameters are listed in Table 2. Firstly, the catalyst was oxidized under the reaction atmosphere of 14% O /N . With the introduction of 1000 ppm NO/N, the content of component I decreases from 53% to 10%, accompanied by the appearance of a Fe2+ site (component V), signifying that the [FeO]+ was reduced to Fe2+. Compared to component I, the insignificant change in QS values of component V points to the [Fe2+-NO −]+ structure maybe formed at the G-site. When 14% O /N was introduced instead of NO, the oxidation reaction from Fe2+ to [FeO]+ took place according to the disappearance of component V in conjunction with the component I increasing from 10% to 52%. Time-resolved in situ FT-IR spectra on 0.6Fe-FER zeolite were also employed as a complementary technique to monitor changes in Fe sites during the NO oxidation reaction. The introduction of 1000 ppm NO/N induced a distinct shift of the T–O–T vibrational peak to higher wavenumbers in IR spectra, suggesting increased formation of Fe2+ species with a significant decrease in the [FeO]+ site. This shift is accompanied by the emergence of IR bands at 1870, 1590, and 1478 cm−1, which are attributed to Fe2+–NO, nitrates, and Fe2+–NO − species, respectively. Accordingly, the IR band at 909 cm−1 can be assigned to T–O–T oxygen bridges perturbed by Fe2+–NO − species. When 14% O /N was introduced instead of NO, a time-dependent shift of the T–O–T vibrational peak to lower wavenumbers was observed, accompanied by the appearance of a band at 1625 cm−1 (attributed to NO adsorption) and a decrease in the Fe2+–NO − species at 1478 cm−1. These observations suggest that NO oxidation proceeds via Fe2+–NO − as an intermediate, as depicted in Fig. 3e, which is in good agreement with the results of the Mössbauer spectra. The significant variance observed in [FeO]+ demonstrates its pivotal role as an active site in the NO oxidation reaction. The [FeO]+ site can react with NO to form [Fe2+-NO −]+ intermediate. Subsequently, NO is generated via electron transfer from NO ⁻ to the oxygen atom (originating from O ), forming the [Fe2+-O−]+ intermediate. Further electron transfer from Fe2+ to O⁻ facilitates the formation of [FeO]+. Time-resolved in situ FT-IR experiment was also conducted to investigate the influence of methanol on Fe sites under reaction conditions. As shown in Fig. S15, the introduction of methanol causes no noticeable change in the perturbed T–O–T vibration of Fe sites, implying that methanol exerts a negligible influence on the iron sites under the reaction conditions.

Methanol-SCR activities were investigated on H-FER zeolite and a series of Fe-FER zeolites. As shown in Fig. 4a, Fe-FER zeolites significantly enhance the catalytic activity at low temperature region (250~350 °C) in comparison with H-FER zeolite. With the increasing Fe content up to 0.6 wt%, the conversion rate of NO at the low temperature region increases gradually with the optimal reaction temperature for the maximum NO conversion (T ) shifting down to a lower temperature (350~300 °C), as shown in Fig. S16. When the Fe content exceeded 0.6 wt%, the catalytic activities gradually decreased at all the entire temperature range. The decrease in the conversion rate of NO on Fe-FER zeolites at high temperature (>300 °C) can be ascribed to the oxidation of methanol to CO and CO , which leads to a shortage of the reductant for the Methanol-SCR reaction, as corroborated by the reaction of methanol oxidation in the absence of NO in Fig. S18. It is noteworthy that Fe-FER zeolite with high iron content (e.g. 1.2 wt%) is more likely to oxidize methanol to CO due to the presence of iron oxide nanoparticles. Meanwhile, under the optimum reaction temperature window (225~300 °C), 0.6Fe-FER zeolite exhibits the best yield of N , accompanied by the least N O formation, as illustrated in Figs. S19 and S20. A progressive increase in iron content leads to a corresponding decline in both deNO activity and N selectivity during the Methanol-SCR reaction, primarily owing to the loss of BASs in the catalysts, as BASs have been reported to be closely associated with the high temperature activity and N selectivity in Methanol-SCR reactions. Moreover, the Fe-FER zeolites exhibit a competitive advantage in low-temperature deNO efficiency compared to other Methanol-SCR catalysts, such as the reported Ag/Ag O and Cu-containing catalysts. The products derived from methanol were also analyzed, as shown in Fig. 4b. Dimethyl ether was readily formed at low temperature (<250 °C) and a small amount of formaldehyde was also detected as by-products in addition to CO and CO . Compared with the serious deactivation of NH -SCR catalysts such as commercial V/W/TiO and Cu-CHA, 0.6Fe-FER zeolite shows only <5% loss of activity at the low temperature region (<300 °C) after withstanding the same SO poisoning treatment as that reported for V/W/TiO catalyst, while the activity at high temperature region (>300 °C) is virtually unaffected. For potential industrial application, the bench test was also conducted under the reaction condition simulating methanol engine exhaust, using a 150×150×150 mm monolithic catalyst coated with 0.6Fe-FER zeolite. As shown in Fig. 4c, the coated monolithic catalyst still remains higher catalytic activity, achieving NO conversion above 80% within the temperature range of 300 to 400 °C, and a remarkable catalytic stability with more than 200 h could also be achieved at 300 °C.

The activation of methanol in zeolite to form methyl groups plays a strikingly important role in the Methanol-SCR reaction on the basis of our previous work. As displayed in Fig. S27, when CH OH and O were introduced, three identical methyl signals at 60.9, 59.2 and 50.5 ppm are observed on both H-FER and 0.6-Fe-FER zeolites corresponding to side-on adsorbed dimethyl ether (DME), methyl groups generated on BAS and adsorbed methanol, respectively. No new methyl signals appeared on 0.6Fe-FER zeolite, signifying that methanol is mainly activated on BASs rather than Fe sites. The adsorption capacity of NO, NO and CH OH molecules on BASs was also explored by DFT calculations. It reveals that the BASs in FER zeolite display a much stronger adsorption capacity for CH OH molecules (25.2 kcal/mol) than that for NO (5.2 kcal/mol) and NO (8.6 kcal/mol), as manifested in Figs. 4e and S28. Together with the results of 13C CP/MAS NMR measurements as illustrated in Fig. S27, it can be reasonably inferred that the BASs will be preferentially occupied by the methanol molecules and further activated to form methyl groups during the Methanol-SCR reaction.

The role of Fe sites in Methanol-SCR reaction
In practical SCR reactions, the abundant presence of water vapor inevitably facilitates the interaction of NO with H O, thereby leading to the formation of nitrites or nitrates that act as reactive intermediates in the overall process. In both NH -SCR and Methanol-SCR processes, HONO has been identified as a crucial nitrogen-containing reaction intermediate, and its formation is also influenced by the NO/NO ratio. Therefore, the formation of HONO on the catalysts was further investigated. Time-resolved in situ Fourier transform infrared (FT-IR) experiments were implemented to further reveal the effect of Fe sites on Methanol-SCR reaction. As shown in Fig. 5a, when NO and O were flowed in, the adsorbed NO (1630 cm−1) was first observed on H-FER zeolite; meanwhile, the adsorbed nitrates (1590 cm−1), N O (1700 cm−1), and NO+NO (2235 cm−1) species appeared gradually. Subsequently, CH OH was introduced in place of NO, and absorption peaks at 1370, 1460, 2855, and 2965 cm−1 corresponding to methyl groups appeared, accompanied by the consumption of absorption peaks at 3590 cm−1 and 3650 cm−1, owing to the absorption and activation of methanol on BAS and EFAL species (Al-OH), respectively. Compared to H-FER zeolite, 0.6Fe-FER zeolite exhibits different adsorption species when NO and O are flowed in. As shown in Fig. 5c, no adsorbed N O species were observed on the 0.6Fe-FER zeolite, while the formation of nitrite (1470 cm−1) was detected. HONO has been proposed as a key intermediate in the SCR reaction over both copper- and iron-containing zeolites, and is also regarded as a nitrite-precursor. However, it is difficult to detect directly as a highly reactive intermediate. Once formed, it is rapidly adsorbed by hydroxyl groups and subsequently converted into nitrite species via reactions such as Al–OH + HONO → Al–ONO + H O. Therefore, nitrite species are generally accepted as indirect evidence for the formation of HONO. In the Methanol-SCR reaction, HONO produced by the interaction of NO with H O corresponds to a general reaction occurring on zeolites: NO+NO +H O→2HONO. In comparison, under dry conditions, more NO+NO and adsorbed NO species were formed on the 0.6Fe-FER zeolite, whereas the adsorbed NO species were not further converted to HONO, as shown in Fig. S32. As the purging process commences, the hydroxyl vibration at ~3650 cm−1 rapidly disappears, whereas the IR absorption band at 1630 cm−1 remains, suggesting that the species responsible for the IR absorption band at 1630 cm−1 is primarily adsorbed NO rather than water. Accordingly, the absence of H O leads to a significant decrease in Methanol-SCR reactivity. Furthermore, when CH OH was introduced instead of NO, the generation and consumption of IR absorption band at 1690 cm−1 can be captured, as manifested in Fig. 5d. Notably, the species with the IR absorption band at 1690 cm−1 is assigned to formamide, another key intermediate in the Methanol-SCR reaction, which can be formed by the conversion of nitromethane resulting from the reaction of methyl groups and adsorbed HONO. These reaction intermediates are consistent with those previously reported for the Methanol-SCR process. With the aid of SVUV-PIMS spectroscopy, Chen et al. found the presence of nitromethane but with a low ion signal strength in the Ethanol-SCR and (NH +Ethanol)-SCR processes. The above elaboration points to the fact that the introduction of Fe sites not only facilitates the oxidation of NO, but also further promotes the generation of the key intermediate HONO, thus enhancing the reactivity of Methanol-SCR. A comprehensive reaction pathway for the Methanol-SCR process was proposed, as depicted in Fig. S34. BASs contribute to the adsorption and activation of methanol to generate active methyl groups, while [FeO]+ sites are conductive to produce HONO, thereby accelerating the generation of the key intermediate nitromethane, which can transform to formamide and subsequently react with NO to produce N .

Since the component III of Fe2+ at G-site is insensitive to oxidizing and reducing treatment and shows little tendency to participate in the reaction, DFT calculations were adopted to further explore the role of Fe3+ and [FeO]+ sites in the formation of HONO. According to the results of Mössbauer spectra, the models of [FeO]+ at the G-site and Fe3+ at the B-site are constructed in FER zeolite, and the reaction pathways for generating HONO are proposed, as depicted in Fig. S35. On the [FeO]+ at G-site, NO first reacts with [FeO]+ to form Fe2+-NO −, then NO − reacts with H O to produce Fe-OH and a HONO with an energy barrier of 26.3 kcal/mol. Afterwards, the Fe-OH should overcome a barrier of 30 kcal/mol, and react with NO to form [FeO]+ and another HONO. The reaction path follow a general reaction in zeolite: NO+NO +H O→2HONO. On the Fe3+ at the B-site, NO is more likely to adsorb on the Fe3+ site first, and a prohibitively high energy barrier (77.5 kcal/mol) need to be overcome to generate HONO (Fig. 5e). The above results suggest that [FeO]+ at the G-site can function as a promoter of HONO production, whereas Fe3+ at the B-site does not. The formed HONO will further react with the activated methyl group at the BAS to produce the key intermediates nitromethane and formamide, thereby enhancing the catalytic performance of Methanol-SCR.

Overall, [FeO]+ is a preferred active site for the NO oxidation and Methanol-SCR. The dynamic evolution of Fe sites provides an interpretation that Fe sites with reactive oxygen are susceptible to the oxidation and reduction treatment, accompanied by variation in the valence state of the Fe sites. Conversely, the respective Fe2+ at the G-site and Fe3+ at the B-site are difficult to activated during the reaction process. Notably, [FeO]+ has two fewer positive charges than Fe3+, so less negative charge is required to balance the [FeO]+ site in the framework of zeolite, which allow more Si-O−-Al sites to be released to produce BASs. BASs also play a critical role in Methanol-SCR. On one hand, methanol can be activated on BASs to generate methyl groups to participate in the reaction. On the other hand, BASs are directly related to N selectivity, as reported in the previous studies. CHA and FER zeolites with a Cu loading of 0.6 wt% were prepared and evaluated for the Methanol-SCR and NO oxidation reaction. The Cu-FER zeolite prepared by the ion exchange method (0.6Cu-FER-IE) exhibits high catalytic activity in the temperature range of 350~450 °C with the conversion of NO above 70%, while the Cu-CHA zeolite, commonly used as a commercial NH -SCR catalyst, showed less than 20% activity across the entire temperature range. The catalytic performance of the Cu-FER zeolite in the Methanol-SCR reaction appear to depend primarily on the BASs of the FER framework, as its activity is similar to that of the H-FER zeolite. Moreover, neither the Cu-FER nor the Cu-CHA zeolite exhibits significant NO oxidation activity. The pronounced difference in activities between the Cu-FER zeolites synthesized by different methods suggest the presence of distinct copper species in the two catalysts, a phenomenon that needs further investigation. A methanol oxidation experiment was also conducted for the Cu-CHA zeolite. As shown in Fig. S36, in contrast to the Fe-FER zeolite, the Cu-CHA zeolite predominantly oxidizes methanol to CO rather than CO, suggesting that the two catalysts exhibit markedly different behaviors in methanol oxidation. This implies that the carbon-containing intermediates formed during the Methanol-SCR process are likely different for these two catalysts. FER zeolite is a medium-pore zeolite consisting of 10-membered ring (4.2×5.4 Å) channels intersected by 8-membered ring (3.5×4.8 Å) channel, whereas the CHA zeolite features a three-dimensional microporous framework composed of cha cages interconnected by eight-membered ring (8-MR) windows (~3.8×3.8 Å). The low activity of the CHA zeolite in the Methanol-SCR reaction is likely attributed to its unique microporous structure, which easily causes carbon deposition during the methanol-related reaction. It indicates that the zeolite topology also plays a crucial role in the Methanol-SCR catalytic performance.

In this work, we have demonstrated that the collaboration of acid sites and iron redox sites in zeolite can promote the low-temperature Methanol-SCR activity on a series of Fe-FER zeolites, which boosts the catalytic activity of Methanol-SCR significantly at low temperature region (250~350 °C). Pilot-scale bench test using the coated monolithic catalyst also exhibited a remarkable NO conversion and a high stability at low temperature, clearly indicating the great potential application of Fe-FER zeolite catalyst in industrial Methanol-SCR. Further mechanistic studies indicated that BASs in FER zeolite could generate methyl groups by activating methanol, whereas an atomically dispersed [FeO]+ site would further improve the redox properties of the Methanol-SCR catalysts by facilitating the oxidation of NO and the generation of key intermediate HONO. This work discloses the similar design principles of SCR catalysts, and deepens the cognition and understanding of the redox sites for SCR reaction. It not only provides a powerful way to design promising Methanol-SCR catalysts, but also offers a guiding direction for the establishment of the structure-activity relationship of such SCR catalysts.

## Methods

Catalyst preparation
FER zeolite catalysts were prepared by the hydrothermal method with pyrrolidine and ethylene glycol as structure-directing agents (SDAs). Firstly, 0.245 g of NaOH and 0.48 g of NaAlO were dissolved in 10 g of H O. Then, 3 g of fumed silica was added to the mixture under rigorous stirring, followed by 21 g of ethylene glycol being dropped in the above solution. The obtained gel was transferred into an autoclave with a PTEE liner for hydrothermal synthesis at 180 °C for 24 h. Subsequently, a mixture prepared by ferric sulfate with different masses and 0.392 g of pyrrolidine dissolved in 3.5 g of H O was added to the cooled gel and continued to hydrothermal synthesis at 180 °C for 72 h. The obtained product was separated, followed by washing with deionized water, drying at 100 °C overnight. Finally, the obtained solid was calcinated in air at 600 °C for 6 h to remove the SDAs and calcined at 550 °C for 2 h followed by ion exchanging with the solution of NH Cl for 3 times to get Fe-FER catalysts. The final product was denoted as xFe-FER, of which the suffix of x referred to the mass percentage of the loading of Fe. H-FER was prepared by a similar procedure except for the addition of ferric sulfate. 0.6Cu-FER-one pot zeolite was successfully synthesized using copper sulfate as the Cu precursor, following the same protocol as 0.6Fe-FER zeolite. Cu-FER-IE and Cu-CHA zeolites were prepared by ion exchanging with the solution of copper acetate. The detailed procedure is as follows: 0.031 g of copper acetate was dissolved in 10 g of H O, followed by the addition of 3 g of NH -FER or NH -CHA zeolite to the copper acetate solution. The mixture was stirred vigorously at 80 °C for 2 h. The resulting Cu-FER-IE or Cu-CHA sample was then obtained by filtration, washed with deionized water, dried at 100 °C overnight, and finally calcined at 550 °C for 2 h.

XRD measurement
The framework of the FER samples was confirmed by powder XRD patterns with Cu Kα radiation (λ=1.5418 Å) and with a scan rate of 2θ=8.0 °/min at 3~55° (Rigaku MiniFlex 600 Benchtop X-ray diffractometer).

Inductively coupled plasma atomic emission spectroscopy (ICP-AES)
The content of Fe present in FER zeolite was determined by ICP-AES (Agilent Technology 4210).

UV-vis spectra
The UV-vis spectra were depicted with a UV-vis spectrophotometer (UV-2600, Shimadzu).

N 2 adsorption and desorption measurement
N adsorption/desorption experiments of samples were performed on 3H-2000PM2 (BEISHIDE), and the samples were degassed under vacuum at 200 °C for 5 h before analysis. Typically, the Brunauer-Emmett-Teller (BET) equation was used to calculate the specific area of the sample, and the micropore specific surface area was evaluated using t-plot method.

TEM
HR-TEM, HAADF, and EDS images were taken using a FEI Talos F200X S/TEM with a field-emission gun at 200 kV. A spherical aberration-corrected HAADF-STEM image was taken by JEM-ARM300F with a field-emission gun at 300 kV. The pores of zeolite and Fe single atom were operated at the accelerating current of 5 µA and 15 µA, respectively.

XAS measurement
Fe K-edge XAS were carried out using a synchrotron radiation ring at PF-12C beamline (Photon Factory, KEK) equipped with a Si(111) single-crystal monochromator in a fluorescence mode. The data analysis of the XAS spectra was conducted by the Demeter software package ATHENA and ARTEMIS. The Fourier transform of the k3-weighted EXAFS was carried out over a k range of 3–10 Å−1. Samples were pretreated to remove the adsorbed water at 200 °C for 2 h in flowing synthetic air before sealing in polyethylene cells for XAS measurements.

In situ Mössbauer spectroscopy measurements
For Mössbauer spectroscopy measurements, 57Fe was introduced into FER zeolites by the above-described methods. The transmission 57Fe Mössbauer spectra were collected at 300 °C using 57Co in Rh matrix as a source. The velocity scale was calibrated using sodium nitroprusside (SNP), and the isomer shift quoted in this work is relative to that of the α-Fe. The spectra were analyzed using the MossWinn software. Prior to the Mössbauer spectra test, all the samples were dehydrated at 500 °C in 14% O /N for 2 h. Thereafter, the reaction gas at a flow of 50 mL/min was introduced at 300 °C for 1 h in the following order: 14% O /N ; 1000 ppm NO/N ; 14% O /N).

NMR measurements
All NMR experiments were performed on a Bruker Avance III 400 MHz spectrometer with resonance frequencies of 400.1 and 100.6 MHz for 1H and 13C, respectively. 1H MAS NMR spectra were collected at a MAS rate of 10 kHz, using a single-pulse excitation of π/2, pulse duration of 2.6 µs, and a repetition time of 20 s. 2D 1H-1H DQ MAS NMR experiments were executed using a POST-C7 pulse sequence with a recycle delay of 20 s and a MAS rate of 10 kHz. 16 scans were acquired for each t1 increment. Note that prior to 1H NMR test, all the samples were dehydrated at 420 °C in vacuum (below 10−3 Pa) for 12 h. 13C CP/MAS NMR spectra were collected using a 4.0 mm HX double resonance MAS NMR probe at a MAS rate of 10 kHz. An number of scans of 1800 and a repetition time of 4 s were used. The samples pelletized in 80-100 mesh were firstly pretreated at 500 °C for 2 h in synthetic air. Thereafter, the reaction gas at a flow of 50 mL/min was introduced at 300 °C CH OH+O (1000 ppm 13CH OH and 7% O in N atmosphere). Finally, the sample was quickly cooled down for 13C NMR measurement.

NH -TPD measurements
NH -TPD experiments were performed on a chemisorption analyzer (PCA-1200 Builder Technology). The samples were pretreated at 400 °C for 1 h in synthetic air with a flow of 50 mL/min to remove the adsorbed water. The temperature was cooled down to 100 °C and saturated with 1% v/v NH /He mixture with a flow rate of 20 mL/min for 1 h. Physisorbed ammonia was removed at 100 °C for 1 h in helium flow until the TCD signal was stabilized. The sample was heated from 100 °C to 700 °C with a 5 °C/min ramping rate in a helium flow rate of 20 mL/min−1. Desorption of NH 3 was monitored by mass spectrometry (m/z=16).

In situ FT-IR spectroscopy
In situ FT-IR experiments were conducted on a Thermal Scientific Nicolet iS10 instrument with a DTGS detector. Infrared spectra were overlapped 16 times at a resolution of 4 cm−1. ~10 mg of the sample was pressed into a slice (0.8 MPa) with a diameter of 13 mm and then transferred to the transmission cell equipped with ZnSe windows. The sample was pretreated at 500 °C for 2 h with a flow of 50 mL/min in synthetic air before the adsorption of the reaction gas. The transient reaction of Methanol-SCR was monitored by FT-IR with gas composition as follows: NO+O (500 ppm NO and 7% O in N atmosphere); CH OH+O (1000 ppm CH OH and 7% O in N atmosphere), and N balanced. Simultaneously, H O was introduced by bubbling with N (1 mL/min) at 30 °C. The total flow rate of gas was 50 mL/min. The background spectrum was collected after the bubbling of H O with N for 30 min before the reaction gas was flowed into the cell to perform in situ measurements. The perturbed T-O-T vibrational modes (1000~800 cm−1 in the IR spectra) of the zeolite framework to distinguish different Fe sites were obtained at 175 °C, and the background spectrum was collected without the sample in the synthetic air. The reducing and oxidizing half reactions of NO oxidation were monitored by FT-IR at 300 °C with gas composition in the following order: 14% O /N ; 1000 ppm NO/N; 14% O /N ). Prior to NH adsorption experiments, the samples were evacuated (10−7 mbar) at 450 °C for 1 h. Then, FTIR spectra were acquired at 150 °C after adsorption of excess NH (10 mbar). Extinction coefficient of 0.11 cm2 µmol−1 for NH + deforming vibration bands (1460 cm−1) and 0.026 cm2 µmol−1 for NH deforming vibration bands (1620 cm−1) in IR spectra as described in previous publications, were employed to calculate the amount of Brønsted acid sites and Lewis acid sites, respectively.

Activity tests
Methanol-SCR reaction was executed in a fixed-bed reactor with the reactant gas mixture containing 2000 ppm CH OH, 1000 ppm NO, 14% O , and 5% H O in N balance. 1000 ppm NO and 14% O were used for the reaction of NO oxidation. The total flow rate of gas through the catalysts was 1000 mL/min with a gas hourly space velocity (GHSV) of 30,000 h−1. CH OH/H O solution was injected by a liquid plunger pump and flew through the evaporator. 2 mL of catalyst used for the catalytic activity test was prepared by pressing the catalyst powders under a pressure of 0.9 MPa, then pelletized and sieved to 18~30 mesh. The temperature was measured in the range of 200 °C to 500 °C. CH OH, CH OCH , CO, CO , NO, NO , and N O of the outlet gas were quantified by an FTIR spectrometer (Nicolet iS10). HCHO of outlet gas was analyzed by a KITAGAWA gas detector tube (Komyo Rikagaku Kogyo). SO poisoning of the Fe-FER catalyst was carried out under the conditions referred to in the previous work.

The bench test was conducted at the Shanghai Marine Diesel Engine Research Institute using a 150×150×150 mm monolithic catalyst coated with 0.6Fe-FER zeolite. The reaction condition refers to methanol engine exhaust parameters containing 2000 ppm CH OH, 1000 ppm NO, 14% O , 10% CO , and 5% H O in N balance with a GHSV of 15,000 h−1. The conversion of NO and N yield were calculated by following equation:

NOx conversion % = (NO xinlet - NO xoutlet) / NO xinlet × 100 %

N 2 yield % = (2 × N 2 outlet) / (NO xinlet + NO xoutlet) × 100 %

Thereaction rate was calculated using the following equation:

Reaction rate (mmol g−1 h−1) = (Feed mL h−1 × X NOx (%)) / (m catal (g) × 22.4 (L mol−1) × 10−3 (mol mmol−1) × 103 (mL L−1))

where Feed NOx represents the concentration of NO , X NOx represents the conversion of NO , m catal represents the mass of catalyst.

Kinetic measurements
The limitations of internal and external diffusion were evaluated by reactions under different gas velocity and grain mesh before the kinetic measurements of the NO oxidation reaction. As shown in Fig. S37a, the conversions of NO are almost unchanged with different particle size from 40~100 mesh under GHSV=30,000 h−1. Thus, internal diffusion limitation was excluded with the particle size of 40~60 mesh. Furthermore, as shown in Fig. S37b, the conversions of NO are almost unchanged with the GHSV≥800,000 h−1 indicating that the external diffusion limitation was also excluded with the GHSV=800,000 h−1. According to the above experiments, the GHSV and particle size were selected as 800, 000 h−1 and 40~60 mesh, respectively. Total gas flow through the catalysts was 1000 mL/min. The Arrhenius plots was drawn according to the reaction rate with the conversion of NO less than 20 %. The reaction order with respect to NO was also determined under the condition at 175 °C, a feed containing 14% O with N as balance gas was used and NO concentrations were varied in the range of 100~900 ppm.

Computation details
The FER zeolite model used for the adsorption of reaction gas was constructed by truncating a 60T cluster from the crystal structure. In order to reduce the computational cost, the computational model employed for the calculation of the reaction path was constructed by truncating an 18T cluster from the 60T cluster. One silicon atoms in the framework were replaced by one aluminum atom to construct H-FER zeolite model. Fe-FER zeolite was modeled by the construction of [FeO]+ and Fe3+ sites at the G-site and B-site, respectively. Atoms far away from the reactants were kept fixed to their equilibrium positions during the optimization process for the skeleton stabilization. All of the associated structures were optimized at the level of DFT with Becke’s three-parameter exchange and Lee-Yang-Parr correlation functional (B3LYP) implemented in the Gaussian 09 package. The pseudo-potential basis set SDD was utilized for Fe, and the polarized 6-31g (d, p) basis set was used for Si, Al, O, H, C, and N atoms. The combination of B3LYP/6-31g (d, p) has been previously reported to provide accurate results in zeolite-catalyzed reactions. Berny algorithms were adopted to search and optimize the transition states. The Hessian matrix was calculated to validate that only one imaginary frequency was observed for each transition state.

## Your Original Review (Round 1)

### Reviewer 1

This paper describes an Fe-FER zeolite which is catalytic for NOx reduction with methanol (MeOH). Several characterization methods were used to characterize the active site of Fe in the FER zeolite. While the NOx conversions are interesting, there are a number of issues that need to be addressed before this paper can be accepted.
Comments:
1. The figures for the characterizations are very small and important features can not be evaluated. In addition, five Fe sites are proposed from the characterizations, which appears to result from overfitting of the data. Justification for the validity of fitting several different sites needs to be justified. The tables report 3 significant figures for Mossbauer (T1 and T2), 4 significant figures for H NMR (TS3) and 3 significant figures for XAS. The small features and noise, which can’t be judged from the figures, would not appear to justify the fits. A more complete analysis of all samples and figures in the SI is required.
2. The number of H+ sites was determined by H NMR (Fig S4 and TS3, for example) and NH3 TPD. The NH3 TPD still has a significant overlap of the physisorbed NH3 with the H+ sites, which makes quantification of the H+ sites inaccurate. Better methods to determine the number of H+ sites by NH3 TPD is necessary. The number of H+ sites should be compared to the NH3 TPD and the Al composition. Without consistency for these results, the data cannot be considered correct.
3. The XAS data is incompletely and poorly fit. What is the pre-edge XANES energy of every sample and reaction condition? The pre-edge energy of Fe+2 and Fe+3 are different. Mossbauer shows a change to more Fe+2 for NO oxidation. Is there a change in the pre-edge peaks. There is also an increase in the formation of more FeO+. Is there a simultaneous increase in the Fe-O CN. What is this bond distance, separate from the Fe states that do not change? If this is the active Fe, then this Fe-O bond distance is important, for example for modeling the catalytic process.
4. The reaction chemistry for NO oxidation does not make sense. Mossbauer show a change in the I peak decreasing from about 45% to 10% (T2). The other sites occupancies remain about the same, within about 5%. A new peak V is fit which increases with NO/O2 and decreases with O2 (T2). (There is no experimental procedure for NO oxidation given in the experimental section and the text and table are unclear of the exact reaction conditions. I assume that NO oxidation has NO + O2.) Peak V is described at Fe+2 with bond NO2 with -1 charge (?). Does NO react at the FeO+ site? If so, why not treat the oxidized catalyst with NO and show the formation of bond NO2. The Mossbauer might show completed loss of Peak 1, with NO at 300C. Then reaction with O2 of this state might regenerate Peak 1. The reaction of O2 often requires multiple active sites, i.e., 2 Fe sites in molecular proximity. ½ O2 is not a reactant as show in Fig. 3d. (If there are 3 significant figures in the Mossbauer fits, then all sites are active, since they change by more than 0.1%!)
5. If FeO+ is the catalytic site, Mossbauer indicates that 0.4, 0.6 and 1.2% Fe have 47, 53 and 45%, respectively. If the fits are good to 5% (not 0.1%) then the number of active sites in all catalysts is similar. Why is the deNOx rate (Fig 4a) of the 1.2% Fe much lower than that of the former samples? Also, why does the rate of the 0.4% Fe remain higher at high T, compared to the other 2 samples?
The catalytic performance for NO oxidation and deNOx reaction needs to be more clearly determined. Kinetic rates, and TOR if FeO+ is the active site, activation energies and how these changes with gas concentrations need to be determined. While deNOx by methanol leads to partially oxidized hydrocarbons, there are readily oxidized to CO2 in a subsequent catalytic step. However, the formation of N2O, which is a much more intensive green house gas than NOx and CO2, will not be attractive for practical applications. While the type of characterizations appears to be sufficient to characterize the active site of catalyst, these methods need to be more thoroughly analyzed and with additional experiments are needed to confirm the active site. With a mixture of Fe states, both oxidation states and site locations, well designed experiments are needed to show which of these site change, and which are inactive. Then the structure of this site needs to be isolated from the spectra in each method. For oxidation reactions (NO oxidation or deNOx) catalyst characterizations for the two half reactions, i.e., reducing and oxidizing half reactions, allow for more accurate identification of the sites that are changing structure and oxidation state.
Additional experiments and analysis are required before this manuscript can be accepted.

### Reviewer 2

This work provides important mechanistic insights into the role of [FeO]⁺ in Methanol-SCR combining experimental and computational approaches to elucidate its function in NO oxidation and HONO formation. While the work is well-structured and presents compelling findings, additional information is required to enhance the study’s robustness. The detailed comments are as follows.
Specific Comments
1. The results from Mössbauer spectroscopy and the CO₂ concentration data from methanol oxidation suggest that a notable proportion of small FexOy species are present in the 1.2Fe-FER catalyst. However, it is interesting to note that no related structural information was observed in other characterization techniques, such as XRD and EXAFS. To provide a more comprehensive understanding, the authors may consider supplementing their discussion with additional analyses, such as Wavelet transform spectra. Furthermore, UV-Vis spectroscopy could be a useful tool to determine the presence of oligomeric Fe species, which would help clarify this point.
2. In Lines 157–163, it would be beneficial for the authors to explicitly clarify which catalyst the IS and QS values of species I, II, and III correspond to. Specifically, do these values represent those of 0.6Fe-FER, or are they averaged across different catalysts? Clarifying this aspect would enhance the readers’ understanding of the presented data.
3. The 2D 1H-1H DQ MAS NMR spectroscopy data of H-FER reveal two distinct cross-peak pairs, which the authors attribute to interactions between adjacent BAS and EFAL sites. The authors further propose that Fe incorporation into BAS sites during hydrothermal synthesis led to the disappearance of autocorrelation peaks. However, it is observed that only one cross-peak pair was significantly affected and converged, while the other remained unchanged. A more detailed discussion on why certain BAS sites were preferentially affected by Fe incorporation would strengthen the interpretation of the NMR results.
4. To further support the discussion on BAS acidity changes, the authors may consider providing FTIR analysis using NH₃ as a probe molecule. Such an analysis would allow for a clearer evaluation of how Fe substitution influences the acidic properties of the catalyst.
5. Since Fe is known to exhibit ammonia decomposition activity at elevated temperatures, it would be valuable for the authors to discuss whether this effect could have influenced the NH₃-TPD results. Providing MS data alongside NH₃-TPD would help confirm whether ammonia decomposition contributed to the observed desorption profiles.
6. To more effectively illustrate the suppression of N₂O formation, the inclusion of N₂ selectivity data, in addition to N₂ yield, would be highly beneficial. Selectivity provides a clearer perspective on how efficiently NOx is converted to N₂ relative to other byproducts, thereby offering a more comprehensive assessment of catalyst performance.
7. In Fig. 4(b), the total carbon concentration at 200°C appears inconsistent with the trend observed in the dataset. Given that CH₃OCH₃ contains two carbon atoms, its contribution to the total carbon balance should be adjusted accordingly. A re-evaluation of this calculation may improve the accuracy of the presented data.
8. The authors propose that the oxidation state of [FeO]⁺ changes CH₃OH-SCR. If this is the case, one might expect corresponding variations in TOT vibrations and M-O stretching vibrations under reaction conditions. Providing additional spectroscopic analyses, such as in situ FTIR or Raman spectroscopy, could further substantiate this claim and strengthen the overall discussion.
9. While this study provides valuable insights into the role of [FeO]⁺ in NO oxidation and Methanol-SCR, the reliance on Mössbauer spectroscopy for Fe species assignment raises some concerns as the deconvolution process could introduce variability in some cases (Fig. 1e). Additionally, XANES data (Fig. 1b) suggest that most of Fe species are observed in the Fe³⁺ oxidation state, which calls for further discussion on the oxidation state assignments. Given that cation location in FER zeolite frameworks is known to influence perturbed vibrational modes (~900 cm⁻¹ in IR), employing IR spectroscopy could provide a complementary method to distinguish Fe site locations, as seen in studies on Co-FER and Pd-FER (There are numerous literatures on this). Furthermore, while the manuscript attributes the superior NO oxidation ability of [FeO]⁺ to its coordinated oxygen, it remains unclear whether this effect is primarily due to reactive oxygen species or intrinsic geometric differences arising from distinct cation positions. Addressing these aspects through additional spectroscopic validation would further strengthen the conclusions of this study.
10. Although the authors claim HONO as a key intermediate in the Methanol-SCR mechanism, additional evidence is required. The presented IR data primarily shows the presence of methyl groups, nitrates, and nitrites, but does not explicitly confirm the formation or participation of HONO in the reaction pathway. I am not sure whether the authors' previous work may provide further justification or not, it would be beneficial to discuss whether HONO can be directly observed through spectroscopic techniques. If direct detection is challenging, exploring indirect validation methods such as isotope labeling experiments or kinetic studies could provide additional support for its role.
11. Lastly, I think a broader comparison with other catalysts should be provided. Since Cu-based zeolites are generally known for their superior redox properties compared to Fe-based ones, they may exhibit even higher activity in this reaction. Including Cu-exchanged zeolite as a reference catalyst could offer useful context for evaluating the advantages and limitations of Fe-FER, particularly regarding NO oxidation and overall Methanol-SCR performance.

### Reviewer 3

This paper reports on a mechanistic study of the Selective Catalytic Reduction of NO over Fe-zeolite catalysts using methanol as the reducing agent. The authors claim that the collaboration between zeolitic acid sites and Fe redox sites provides a strategy for boosting the low-T MeOH SCR activity: however, I have some doubts about the novelty of this concept and the conclusive nature of the evidence included in the manuscript. Please see my points below.
1. As a preliminary general comment, the English usage needs to be improved: there are several incomplete or incorrect sentences and typos, which make sometimes difficult to follow the text flow.
2. A major concern is the identification of the oxidation of NO to NO2 as the rate limiting step of the SCR reactions (line 188). This is a controversial assumption, which has been shown in the past to contradict several experimental findings. For example, i) the rate of NO oxidation is typically much lower than the SCR rate, ii) H2O has opposite effects on the rates of NO oxidation and of the NH3-SCR reaction, iii) the NO oxidation activities of Fe-zeolite and Cu-zeolite catalysts do not correlate with the corresponding NH3-SCR activities ….
3. Figure 3b shows a linear correlation between the NO oxidation rate at 300°C and the amount of [FeO]+. Notice that at 300°C the NO oxidation rate is already clearly limited by chemical equilibrium: see Figure 3a where the NO conversion at 300°C is in the descending branch of the lightoff curves for all the catalysts. Therefore, the rates plotted in Figure 3b are hardly representative of the intrinsic NO oxidation kinetics, being at least in part controlled by thermodynamics.
4. How were the NO oxidation rates extracted from the integral NO conversion data of Figure 3a?
5. Apparently, the authors propose a NO activation pathway wherein NO is first oxidized to NO2 over [FeO]+ and then HONO is formed. NO oxidation to NO2 is a two-electron process, so how can it proceed over single Fe sites, which cycle between Fe3+ and Fe2+? Can you rule out an alternative pathway where NO is directly oxidized to HONO over Fe3+OH, as proposed in the literature for both Fe- and Cu-zeolite catalysts?

### Reviewer 1

The revised manuscript has been improved; however, several questions remain to be addressed before the manuscript can be accepted.
Comments:
1. From the in situ Mossbauer is it is clear that Peak I, which is assigned to FeO+, is redox active for NO oxidation. The fraction of Peak I decreases on reaction with NO with formation of a new Peak V and oxidizes back to Peak I with O2. The in situ reaction, however, is not MeOH SCR. It’s unfortunate, that the NO reduced Peak V species was not reacted with MeOH and shown to make N2 and the original oxidized Fe, i.e., Peak I. Why does the confirmation of the active site for NO oxidation lead to identification of the active species for MeOH SCR? The connection between the two reactions is not clearly discussed.
2. The XAS analysis is incomplete with little discussion of the results. The XANES pre-edge peak was fit with Fe+2, Fe+3 and Fe2O3. It is not clear what was used for the Fe+2 and Fe+3 standards. Additionally, Fe2O3 has a higher shell Fe-O-Fe peak, see figure 1e, while samples have no higher shell peaks, also see figure 1e. Why is there a good fit of the small pre-edge peak using and incorrect standard? The fractional agreement of Peak III (Fe+2) by Mossbauer with the XANES pre-edge peak is a reasonable agreement for the 0.6% Fe sample. What about the other samples where the Mossbauer has been done, Table 1. Why is there any agreement since you don’t have pure samples? Have these small peaks been overfit?
3. The EXAFS of one sample has been fit. The Fe-O CN was 4.7, Table S3. All the Fe references have 6 Fe-O bonds, so what does it mean when the CN is 4.7? Since there are multiple Fe species by Mossbauer, what information does the bond distance and CN provide? The small size of the FT of the EXAFS, figure S4 is difficult to see if any of the samples are different. From the Mossbauer, there should be significant differences between the samples.
4. In previous work, it has been proposed that HONO species are important reaction intermediates. However, these were shown to be formed by NOx and H2O, see line 340. Why not conduct Mossbauer to show that FeO+ reduced to the reaction intermediate with NOx and H2O? H2O often has a large effect on deNOx chemistry and dry NO may not give the same results as NO + H2O. How has HONO been shown to be the active species for N2 formation (in this study) that is different from previous studies?
5. IR seems to imply that additional reaction intermediates are formed prior to N2 formation. Mossbauer of the same reactions would provide confirmation of the proposed intermediates.
6. If FeO+ is the deNOx active site, the fraction in each sample is approximately the same, Table 1. I don’t understand why having more sites, i.e., same fraction, but higher Fe loading leads to lower rates. The explanation that MeOH is oxidized with high loadings, but not low, doesn’t make sense. If MeOH oxidation is high and nearly completely oxidized with high loadings, but not low loadings, this indicates that high MeOH with higher loaded catalysts will have higher rates. It also suggests that significant oxidation of MeOH will occur on these catalysts. To get high NOx conversions, large amounts of MeOH will be required. This will become a practical problem. I would like to see the highly loaded Fe catalysts kinetics at the same MeOH outlet concentration as that of the low loaded catalysts. Are the TOR the same (based on FeO+)? This would also confirm the active site is FeO+.
7. The oxidation of MeOH would also suggest that other C species may be the reactants, e.g. CO or H2CO. MeOH oxidation would also suggest that FeO+ is partially reduced. How does one know other Fe species are not formed and are the active site? In situ Mossbauer, which is the very interesting part of this paper, could be highly informative.
The conformation of the active site as FeO+, or Fe species formed by reaction with MeOH, can be confirmed by testing each condition at differential conversions and determining the TOR. The amount of MeOH in the outlet gas needs to be high and approximately the same.

### Reviewer 2

We sincerely thank the authors for thoroughly addressing the requested additional analyses. Many of the previous concerns have been sufficiently clarified. However, a few points still remain open to discussion, and we would like to offer some additional comments in this regard.
Specific Comments
1. It is noted that the concentration of CH₃OCH₃ in Fig. 4b has been modified. However, my initial concern was related to a potential error in the calculation or reporting of the total carbon concentration, not in the raw data value of CH₃OCH₃ itself. Therefore, the revision of the CH₃OCH₃ concentration is rather unexpected. To clarify this point, I would appreciate it if the authors could provide the corresponding real-time FTIR data supporting this experiment.
2. Regarding the revised Fig. 3 (the in-situ FT-IR spectra): While I agree with the overall experimental design, I would kindly ask the authors to present the in-situ FT-IR spectra as a time-resolved overlay (with at least 1-minute intervals). the in-situ FT-IR is a powerful technique for tracking the dynamic evolution of surface species in real time. For example, during the gas-switching step from NO to O₂, observing the time-dependent shift of the T–O–T vibrational peak would provide stronger evidence for the proposed consumption of the Fe–NO₂ intermediate. Presenting the data in a time-resolved manner would substantially strengthen the authors’ mechanistic interpretation.
3. We appreciate the authors’ effort in preparing and evaluating two types of Cu ion-exchanged catalysts in response to our previous request. However, we believe that the superior performance of the Fe-FER catalyst is likely attributable to the in-situ incorporation of Fe ions during the hydrothermal synthesis, which enables atomic-level dispersion within the zeolite framework. Therefore, if feasible, we kindly encourage the authors to synthesize a Cu-based catalyst using the same synthetic protocol as that of Fe-FER—by simply replacing the Fe precursor with a Cu precursor. This would allow for a more meaningful and direct comparison between the two metal systems under identical synthetic and structural conditions.

### Reviewer 3

I am satisfied with the authors' response to my comments, but for Comment 3.
In this respect, please notice that the best fit straight line of the reaction rates in the updated Fig. 3b does not pass through the origin. It seems therefore that the rate of NO oxidation is at least in part controlled by something else than just the amount of [FeO]+ sites.
Accordingly, I am even more convinced that the oxidation of NO to NO2 may not be the best reaction to probe the redox properties of the Fe-FER catalyst. Again, the correlation of the NO oxidation activity with the SCR DeNOx activity remains questionable.
These aspect deserve some more thorough discussion in my view.
